La clasificación automática de textos po: Automatic classification of texts by probabilities was proposed by Melvin Maron in 1961, in a paper on automatic document indexing. The application to junk mail arrived in 1998 with a work by Mehran Sahami and his collaborators, but what made it universal was an essay by Paul Graham of August 2002, A Plan for Spam, which told the method in plain language and caused it to be implemented in almost every mail client within months. It is one of the few cases in which you can date precisely the moment a statistical method changed many people's daily lives.

The second reads: “the score of B is the logarithm of P of B, plus the sum of the logarithms of P of w sub i given B”.

Since the logarithm is increasing, comparing scores is the same as comparing probabilities: the class that wins in logarithms wins without them too. And as a bonus, each word contributes a summand, so you can see how much each one pushes to each side. The logarithms of numbers smaller than 1 are negative, so the scores come out negative and the less negative one wins.
Se lee: <em>«la probabilidad de be dado:
It reads: “the probability of B given t equals the probability of t given B, times that of B, over that of t”. Here $B$ is “it is spam” and $t$ is “the text is this one”.

The denominator $P(t)$ is the same for both classes, so to decide which wins it does not have to be computed: comparing the numerators is enough. That saves the hardest part of the calculation, and it is the reason the method is so cheap.
Se lee: <em>«la probabilidad del texto d:
It reads: “the probability of the text given B is approximately the product, over the words, of the probability of word i given B”. The symbol $\prod$ is a product of many factors, as $\sum$ is a sum.

It is the independence condition from [[pe-condicionada|conditional probability]], $P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, applied to all the words at once. And now each factor can be counted: how many times that word comes up in the junk emails, divided by the total.
Se lee: <em>«pe de doble uve dado be es:
It reads: “P of w given B is the times it appears plus one, over the total plus V”, where $V$ is the vocabulary's size.

One appearance is given to every word, even to those that never came up. That way no probability is zero, the denominator is adjusted so that they all still add to 1, and an unknown word weighs little instead of vetoing everything. It is the same idea Laplace used to estimate the probability that the sun will rise tomorrow.
